Soup Joumou

Served at: Fete de Papa Zaka - Feast of the Farmer Loa

Serves 8-10Prep 45 minCook 2 hours 30 min

Soup Joumou, a vibrant and hearty pumpkin soup, is a cornerstone of Haitian culinary tradition. While famously enjoyed on New Year's Day to celebrate freedom, its rich flavors and nourishing ingredients also make it a perfect offering for Fete de Papa Zaka, the Feast of the Farmer Loa. This soup, brimming with the bounty of the earth, honors Papa Zaka's role in providing sustenance and a plentiful harvest, symbolizing gratitude for the land's gifts.

Ingredients

  • 2 lbs (900g) beef stew meat, cut into 1-inch (2.5 cm) cubes
  • 1 lime, juiced
  • 2 tablespoons white vinegar
  • 1 teaspoon salt, plus more to taste
  • 1/2 teaspoon black pepper, plus more to taste
  • 1/2 cup (120ml) epis (Haitian seasoning base, or blend of garlic, onion, bell pepper, parsley, thyme)
  • 2 tablespoons olive oil
  • 2 lbs (900g) calabaza squash (or kabocha), peeled, seeded, and cubed
  • 8 cups (1.9L) water or beef broth
  • 2 medium carrots, peeled and sliced
  • 2 medium potatoes, peeled and cubed
  • 1 cup (150g) chopped cabbage
  • 1 stalk celery, sliced
  • 1 leek, white and light green parts, sliced
  • 1 small turnip, peeled and cubed (optional)
  • 1 small Scotch bonnet pepper, whole (do not break open unless you want it spicy)
  • 2 sprigs fresh thyme
  • 1/4 cup (60ml) chopped fresh parsley
  • 1/2 cup (50g) small pasta (e.g., macaroni, vermicelli, or small shells)
  • 1/4 cup (60ml) fresh lime juice, for finishing

Method

  1. Rinse the beef cubes thoroughly with lime juice and vinegar, then rinse again with cold water. Pat dry with paper towels.
  2. In a large bowl, season the beef with 1 teaspoon salt, 1/2 teaspoon black pepper, and 1/4 cup (60ml) of the epis. Mix well and let marinate for at least 30 minutes, or preferably overnight in the refrigerator.
  3. Heat olive oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Add the marinated beef in batches, browning on all sides. Remove browned beef and set aside.
  4. Add the cubed squash to the pot. Cook for about 5-7 minutes, stirring occasionally, until slightly softened and lightly browned.
  5. Return the browned beef to the pot with the squash. Add the remaining 1/4 cup (60ml) epis and stir to combine.
  6. Pour in 8 cups (1.9L) of water or beef broth. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat to low, cover, and simmer for 1 hour, or until the beef is tender.
  7. Carefully remove about half of the cooked squash from the pot and blend it with a little of the cooking liquid until smooth. Return the blended squash puree to the pot. This will thicken the soup.
  8. Add carrots, potatoes, cabbage, celery, leek, turnip (if using), the whole Scotch bonnet pepper, and thyme sprigs to the pot. Stir well.
  9. Continue to simmer, covered, for another 30-40 minutes, or until all vegetables are tender.
  10. Add the small pasta to the soup and cook according to package directions, usually 8-10 minutes, until al dente.
  11. Remove the Scotch bonnet pepper and thyme sprigs. Stir in the chopped fresh parsley and the final 1/4 cup (60ml) fresh lime juice.
  12. Taste and adjust seasoning with more salt and pepper as needed. Serve hot.

Tips

  • For a richer flavor, you can brown the beef bones (if available) before adding the meat and then simmer them with the water for the first hour.
  • If you prefer a spicier soup, you can prick the Scotch bonnet pepper a few times with a fork before adding it, or carefully slice it open (wear gloves!).
  • Epis is key to Haitian cooking; it can be made by blending garlic, onion, bell pepper, parsley, thyme, and a little olive oil and vinegar. It keeps well in the fridge for a week.
